title: You Put a Ring on Her Finger—So Why Are You Still Courting Other Women?
paragraphs: You Put a Ring on Her Finger—So Why Are You Still Courting Other Women?
You may never have slept with another woman. You may have never kissed her. You may even insist, “Nothing happened.” But Jesus asks a more frightening question: What has been happening in your heart?
There is a kind of adultery that never checks into a hotel.
It never leaves lipstick on a collar. Never produces a suspicious receipt. Never creates a photograph someone can expose.
Sometimes it begins with a notification.
A message.
A reaction to her story.
A conversation you know you would explain differently if your wife were standing beside you.
Sometimes it sounds harmless.
“You look beautiful.”
“I've always admired you.”
“My marriage has been difficult lately.”
“You understand me in a way she doesn't.”
And perhaps nothing physical has happened.
Yet.
That word matters.
Because long before two bodies meet in a forbidden room, two hearts can begin walking toward one.

And if you are a married man who is still deliberately attracting, pursuing, flirting with, emotionally courting, or keeping romantic possibilities alive with other women, this may be one of the hardest things you read today:
The question is not merely whether you have technically committed physical adultery.
The question is why you are nurturing something that belongs inside your covenant.
Jesus refused to let people hide behind technical innocence.
He said:

“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
—Matthew 5:27–28, KJV
The Greek of Matthew 5:28 makes the warning even more penetrating:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn
The idea is not that merely noticing another person's beauty automatically makes someone an adulterer. Jesus is not condemning the involuntary awareness that another human being is attractive.
Temptation and consent are not identical.
The danger is the cultivated look.
The entertained desire.
The inward reaching.
The deliberate feeding of sexual or romantic appetite toward someone who is not your spouse.
That distinction matters, because otherwise sincere Christians can become crushed by condemnation simply because they experienced temptation.
You can be married and notice that another woman is attractive.
The battle begins with what you do next.
Do you surrender the thought to Christ?
Or do you invite it inside, give it a chair, pour it a drink, and ask it to stay?
Because there is an enormous difference between temptation knocking on the door and you preparing a bedroom for it.
And courting another woman while you are married is not merely noticing beauty.
Courting is movement.
It is intentional attention.
It is creating emotional or romantic possibility.
It is communicating, explicitly or implicitly, There may be something between us.
And Scripture does not give a married Christian permission to maintain a wife at home while auditioning alternatives in his heart.
Maybe that sentence hurts.
Keep reading.
Because this is not a story about God catching you so He can destroy you.
This is about Christ confronting what is destroying you so He can call you home.
Maybe your marriage has become painfully ordinary.
The conversations are about bills.
Children.
Deadlines.
Groceries.
Appointments.
Who forgot to pay something.
Who is too tired tonight.
You remember when your wife used to look at you differently.
You remember when you couldn't stop talking.
Now she is exhausted.
You're exhausted.
Then another woman appears.
She laughs at your jokes.
She notices your accomplishments.
She listens.
She compliments you.
She hasn't lived with your weaknesses for fifteen years.
She hasn't watched you fail.
She doesn't know how irritable you become when you're tired.
She knows the edited version of you.
And you know the edited version of her.
That is part of what makes forbidden attraction intoxicating.
Fantasy never has to take out the garbage.
Fantasy never gets sick.
Fantasy never wakes up stressed about money.
Fantasy doesn't have years of unresolved arguments attached to it.
You compare your wife's unedited reality with another woman's carefully framed moments, and suddenly you begin believing you married the wrong person.
But you are comparing a covenant to a fantasy.
And fantasy almost always wins when reality is forced to compete on fantasy's terms.
Then something even more dangerous happens.
You begin rewriting your marriage so your temptation feels justified.
“She doesn't appreciate me.”
“We haven't been close for years.”
“She changed.”
“I deserve to feel wanted.”
“We're basically roommates.”
“God knows how lonely I am.”
Perhaps some of those wounds are real.

A struggling marriage should not be mocked or minimized. Emotional neglect can hurt deeply. Sexual difficulties can be devastating. Betrayal, contempt, constant conflict, or years of disconnection can leave enormous wounds requiring wise pastoral help, counseling, repentance, patience, boundaries, and sometimes serious intervention.
But another woman's attention is not God's prescription for your wounded marriage.
Her affection cannot become medicine for pain that must be brought into the light.
Because sin has always been skilled at turning legitimate hunger into illegitimate permission.
You can be genuinely lonely...
and still be wrong to court another woman.
You can be genuinely wounded...
and still be responsible for what you do with the wound.
You can feel neglected...
and still be called to holiness.
Your pain deserves attention.
It does not deserve a mistress.
And sometimes the affair begins long before anyone calls it an affair.
It begins when she becomes the first person you want to tell.
When you delete messages.
When you hide notifications.
When you wait for her name to appear on your phone.
When you dress hoping she'll notice.
When you tell her things about your marriage that create emotional intimacy between you.
When you imagine what life might have been like if you had met her first.
When you begin protecting the relationship from your spouse's eyes.
Perhaps one brutally simple question exposes everything:
Would you communicate with this woman exactly the same way if your wife were reading every word beside you?
If the answer is no, don't rush past that.
Something is already asking for darkness.
And the Gospel keeps calling things into the light.
Scripture does not merely tell husbands what to avoid. It gives them something infinitely more demanding to become.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
—Ephesians 5:25, KJV
Read those last words again.
Gave himself.
Biblical husbandhood is cruciform.
Christ does not tell a husband merely to remain legally married.
He calls him toward self-giving love.
That means the Christian vision of marriage is radically different from, “Stay until somebody more exciting appears.”
Jesus Christ did not love His church because His church was always easy to love.
He loved sacrificially.
Faithfully.
Covenantally.
And the husband is commanded to look toward Christ as the pattern for loving his wife.
Proverbs says something our novelty-addicted culture desperately needs to hear:
“Rejoice in the wife of thy youth.”
—Proverbs 5:18, KJV
The surrounding passage intentionally directs a husband's sexual delight toward his wife rather than toward forbidden women.
Not merely tolerate her.
Not merely provide money for her.
Not merely remain legally attached to her while giving your emotional electricity to somebody else.
Rejoice in her.
There is something profoundly countercultural about a man deciding:
I will cultivate desire where I made covenant.
I will water my own garden.
I will stop feeding fantasies that make my real marriage look dull.
I will learn my wife again.
I will pursue her again.
I will repent where I have neglected her.
I will listen without defending myself.
I will become curious about the woman sleeping beside me instead of becoming fascinated by the woman I barely know.
I will stop expecting excitement to happen accidentally and start investing intentionally.
Because perhaps your wife isn't the only one who changed.
Maybe you did too.
Maybe somewhere between the wedding photographs and the mortgage, you stopped courting the woman you married...
and started wondering why marriage stopped feeling like courtship.
Then another woman came along, and suddenly you remembered how to compliment.
How to listen.
How to dress well.
How to ask questions.
How to send thoughtful messages.
How to be interesting.
And there is a painful possibility some men need to consider:
What if you are giving another woman the version of yourself your wife has been begging to see again?
That one lands differently.
Because maybe the problem is not simply that another woman became interesting.
Maybe you stopped being intentional at home.
And now you are spending outside the marriage what belongs inside it.
Your attention.
Your imagination.
Your tenderness.
Your curiosity.
Your romantic energy.
Your words.
Your emotional vulnerability.
Your pursuit.
Your wife may be receiving whatever is left after another woman has already received the excitement.
That is why Hebrews treats marriage with tremendous seriousness:
“Marriage should be honored by all, and the marriage bed kept pure.”
Marriage is not merely paperwork.
It is covenant.
And covenant faithfulness matters to God.
But now we need to speak to the man who has already crossed lines.
Maybe this isn't theoretical anymore.
Maybe you already flirted.
Maybe the messages became explicit.
Maybe you've been emotionally involved for months.
Maybe you've kissed her.
Maybe you've slept with her.
Maybe your wife doesn't know.
Maybe she does.
Maybe your marriage is hanging by a thread because of what you did.
And perhaps right now shame is whispering:
You hypocrite.
You ruined everything.
God is finished with you.
There is no coming back from this.
Listen carefully.
The Bible never makes adultery small.
But the Gospel never makes Christ's mercy small either.
Those two truths must remain together.
Grace is not God pretending your sin didn't matter.
Grace is God providing in Christ what sinners could never provide for themselves.
At the cross, Jesus did not die because humanity's sin was insignificant.
He died because sin was deadly.
The cross simultaneously destroys our excuses and destroys our despair.
You cannot stand beneath the cross saying, “My sin isn't serious.”
Look at what redemption cost.
But neither can the repentant sinner stand beneath the cross saying, “My sin is too great for Jesus.”
Look at who is hanging there.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that says, “Keep the other woman and keep Jesus too.”
Not grace that baptizes secrecy.
Not grace that protects your image while your wife bleeds.
Biblical grace teaches us to leave darkness.
Repentance is not feeling terrible because you were caught.
Repentance is a turning.

It means bringing sin into the light before God, ending what must be ended, refusing to continue feeding the relationship, accepting accountability, pursuing truth, and seeking wise biblical and professional help where necessary.
It may mean blocking a number.
Ending private meetings.
Changing routines.
Removing access.
Giving up secrecy.
Confessing without blaming your wife for your choices.
Getting pastoral accountability.
Seeking qualified marriage counseling.
Allowing trust to be rebuilt on your wife's timetable rather than demanding immediate forgiveness because you apologized.
There may be consequences.
Grace does not always erase consequences.
But consequences are not proof that Christ has abandoned the repentant sinner.
Sometimes restoration begins with the terrifying sound of truth finally being spoken.
And if you have not crossed the physical line yet, don't congratulate yourself while continuing to walk toward the cliff.
Jesus' language in Matthew 5:29–30 is deliberately severe: if something causes you to stumble into sin, deal with it radically.
The point is not casual self-mutilation.
The point is ruthless repentance.
Stop negotiating with what is killing your faithfulness.
Don't ask how close you can stand to adultery without technically becoming an adulterer.
Ask how fiercely you can protect what God has entrusted to you.
Maybe that means tonight you stop messaging her.
Maybe you unfollow the account.
Maybe you tell another mature Christian man the truth.
Maybe you hand over the secret you have been protecting.
Maybe you stop telling yourself, “We're only friends,” when you know perfectly well you would be devastated if your wife had the same relationship with another man.
And perhaps the deepest repentance is not simply saying goodbye to another woman.
Perhaps it is learning to turn your face toward your wife again.
Look at her.
Not as furniture in your familiar life.
Not merely as the mother of your children.
Not as the woman who knows your flaws.
Look at the person who stood before God and entrusted part of her future to you.
Remember her laughter.
Remember the nervous excitement.
Remember the first conversations.
Remember what made you choose her.
Then understand something even deeper:
Biblical marriage cannot survive forever on nostalgia.
You must choose faithfulness today.
Love eventually becomes more than something you feel.
It becomes something you practice when feelings fluctuate.
That doesn't make love less beautiful.
It can make love deeper.
The world says the great romance is finding someone who continually gives you butterflies.
Covenant teaches a harder beauty:
Sometimes the great romance is choosing the same person after the butterflies have gone quiet... and discovering that roots can grow deeper than wings ever flew.
And if your marriage is deeply damaged, faithfulness does not mean pretending everything is fine.
Get help.
Have difficult conversations.
Seek wise pastoral counsel.
Seek competent marriage counseling.
Address abuse, betrayal, addiction, contempt, sexual dysfunction, emotional abandonment, or whatever is actually happening rather than covering it with Christian clichés.
And where there is abuse or danger, faithfulness does not require silently remaining unsafe; seek appropriate professional, pastoral, and legal support.
But do not use a broken marriage as permission to build a secret romance.
Bring the brokenness into the light.
Bring your loneliness into the light.
Bring your sexual frustration into the light.
Bring your disappointment into the light.
Bring the other woman's name into the light.
Bring your fantasies into the light.
Bring your phone into the light.
Bring yourself into the light.
Because Jesus Christ does some of His most astonishing rewriting with stories people thought were already ruined.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples fled.
Paul carried a violent past.
The early church was filled not with people who had never needed mercy, but with sinners transformed by Christ.
That doesn't excuse what you have done.
It means what you have done does not have to become the final author of who you are.
Sin may have written a terrible chapter.
Jesus Christ still holds the pen of redemption.
This is From Scandal to Grace.
Not scandal denied.
Scandal confessed.
Not consequences avoided.
Grace encountered.
Not lust renamed “connection.”
Lust surrendered.
Not another secret relationship hidden behind a Christian profile.
A heart finally exposed before Jesus.
Maybe you came into this article defending yourself.
Maybe somewhere halfway through, you stopped.
Maybe one woman's name has been sitting in your mind throughout every paragraph.
You know exactly who she is.
And maybe you know exactly what Christ is asking you to surrender.
Conviction is a mercy when it drives us toward Christ.
Go to Jesus.
Not after you have cleaned yourself enough to become presentable.
Now.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Ask Him for the courage to make what is crooked straight.
Ask Him to teach you how to become faithful in private, not merely respectable in public.
And then take concrete action.
Because there may be a wife somewhere in your house who does not need to compete with every woman who makes you feel admired.
She needs a husband whose heart is learning to come home.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to publish the details of another person's life. But you can stop pretending.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance is possible and Jesus still restores broken people.
Not because saving a post changes a heart, but because there may be a night when temptation starts rewriting the story again and you need to remember what you decided in the light.

Supporting Gospel work financially does not purchase God's blessing, prove your salvation, or make you more spiritual. We glorify God through Christ-centered obedience, generosity, truth, worship, love, and faithful stewardship.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen.
Go home in your heart.
Close the door that should never have been opened.
Turn toward your covenant.
And above everything else, turn toward Christ.
Because your greatest hope is not becoming a man strong enough never to be tempted.

Your greatest hope is Jesus Christ—the Savior strong enough to forgive the repentant, expose darkness, break chains, transform desires, teach faithfulness, heal what sin has wounded, and make sinners new.
Maybe the story became scandalous.
Maybe you helped write the scandal.
But if you will bring the truth into the light and surrender yourself to Christ, the scandal does not have to write the final sentence.
The woman you need to stop pursuing may not be the end of your story; surrendering her may be the moment Jesus begins teaching your heart how to come home.
